'''Stuart Pivar''' (born 1930) is an American chemist and [[art collector]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Steinberg|first=Claudia|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/09/09/garden/two-scientists-caught-in-amber.html|title=Two Scientists Caught in Amber|date=2004-09-09|work=The New York Times|access-date=2020-02-13|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theartnewspaper.com/news/art-collector-who-perished-in-trump-tower-blaze-remembered-as-expert-in-pop-art|title=Art collector who perished in Trump Tower blaze remembered as 'expert' in Pop art|last=Tully|first=Judd|date=April 10, 2018|website=The Art Newspaper|access-date=2020-02-13}}</ref> Trained as a scientist, Pivar has long endorsed the study of anatomy and need for artists to acquire technical skills. He grew his fortune in the plastics industry and is also the author of several books. Pivar is one of the founders of the [[New York Academy of Art]] with, among others, [[Andy Warhol]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Connoly |first=John |date=April 8, 1996 |title=School for Scandal |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NOECAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA24 |journal=New York Magazine |pages=24}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Stuart Pivar was born 1930 in [[Brooklyn]], New York to a father who imported velvet ribbons and a mother known for being "intensely style-conscious".<ref name=":1" />  Pivar speaks [[Yiddish]] and was brought up in a Jewish family.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|last=Fishman|first=Boris|url=https://forward.com/news/4563/dustup-offers-rare-peek-at-trade-in-hate-art/|title=Dustup Offers Rare Peek at Trade in Hate Art|date=November 26, 2004|work=The Forward|access-date=February 12, 2020}}</ref> He began collecting objects at age 7, starting with insects in Central Park, and later bottle caps on [[Kings Highway (Brooklyn)|Kings Highway]]<ref name=":2" /> at age 8.<ref name=":1" />  He spent time at a summer camp in Kingston, New York.  Pivar attended [[Brooklyn Technical High School]] before going on to earn a [[Bachelor of Science|B.Sc]] in chemistry at [[Hofstra University]], graduating in 1951.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d3BzGGApYnEC&q=Stuart+Pivar+chemtainer+Industries&pg=PA122|title=On the Origin of Form: Evolution by Self-Organization|publisher= North Atlantic Books |isbn=978-1-55643-886-8|last=Pivar|first=Stuart|date=2009|access-date=February 12, 2020|page=122}}</ref>

== Career ==
In 1959, Pivar founded Chemtainer Industries, a business that specialized in bulk-storage [[plastic container]]s.<ref name=":1" /> As an inventor, he made a large fortune in plastics. While remaining active in the [[plastics industry]], he became an independently wealthy investor and buyer on the art scene.<ref>Paul Alexander, ''Death and disaster: the rise of the Warhol empire and the race for Andy's millions'', Villard Books, 1994, p.14.</ref>

=== New York Academy of Art ===
Pivar endorsed the reintroduction of traditional skills into art school curricula, including the study of human and animal anatomy. With Warhol, he helped to found the [[New York Academy of Art]] in 1980, becoming one of its board members.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Connoly |first=John |date=April 8, 1996 |title=School for Scandal |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NOECAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA24 |journal=New York Magazine |pages=24}}</ref> The academy opposed [[abstract art]] and promoted traditional skills. According to [[Eliot Goldfinger]], Pivar "strongly supported the acquisition of an anatomical collection of comparative skeletons, related artwork, anatomical models and charts, and the use of dissection as part of the curriculum."<ref>Eliot Goldfinger, ''Animal anatomy for artists: the elements of form'', Oxford University Press, 2004, p.ix.</ref> He donated over $1.2 million to the Academy during his involvement with it.<ref name="conn">
{{Cite journal |last=Connolly |first=J. |date=8 April 1996 |title=How could it be that board members at the New York Academy of Art were too busy fighting with each other to notice that $175,000 was missing? |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NOECAAAAMBAJ&q=%22Stuart+Pivar%22&pg=PA24 |journal=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |page=24}}</ref>

Pivar resigned from the Academy in 1994 and complained that he had been "lied to and outmaneuvered" by other senior figures at the institution. A report placed most of the blame on his "disruptive, angry and abusive" behavior for problems at the institution.<ref name="conn" /> Pivar attempted to sue the Academy for $50 million, claiming that he had been caused "emotional and mental distress" and that he had been ostracised for pointing out falsification of financial records and employment of illegal immigrants.<ref name="50mildolsuit">{{Cite journal |last1=New York Media |first1=LLC |date=1 Dec 1997 |title=Stuart Pivar's New $50 million Suit |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DOgCAAAAMBAJ&q=Stuart+Pivar&pg=PA25 |journal=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |page=25}}</ref> Pivar has stated that he resigned from the Academy Board along with Caroline Newhouse.<ref name="50mildolsuit" />

=== Biological theories ===
Beginning with his book ''Lifecode'' in 2004 Pivar has published novel claims about the evolution of species. He asserts that the body form of [[species]] are encoded not in [[DNA]] but in the patterned structure of a primordial [[germ plasm]].<ref>On the Origin of Form: Evolution by Self-Organization, Stuart Pivar, North Atlantic Books, 2009 {{ISBN|1-55643-886-9}}</ref><ref name="Macmenamin">[https://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&q=cache:CU2gyUDK2twJ:www.ilasol.org.il/ILASOL/uploads/files/ILASOLintroductionV6.pdf+stuart+pivar+evolution&hl=en&pid=bl&srcid=ADGEESgA0o56t0DdMsclymOItS6OIWzPV56kTS3wQLD-PR3oVeFoSq65ffq6ao3hpRCK2uIO_Xa2GIXgXb5FRAQtfEmXVnsEKZbjvoN4FK6Toiybb6Y2855TZQhmxR0tCF84NG0A9cFc&sig=AHIEtbRqUvyz5yqYuyyf9A9wINXZDT3ynQ ILAOL introduction by Mark Macmenamin]</ref> However, critics have stated that Pivar's proposed developmental sequences bear no resemblance to anything actually observed during embryological development.<ref name="Macmenamin" /> In his book on the [[demarcation problem]], ''Nonsense on Stilts'', [[Massimo Pigliucci]] says that he and his graduate students received "more or less threatening" emails from Pivar complaining that his non-novel theory ([[scare quotes|written in quotes]]) of form was not being taken seriously.<ref name="Pigliucci2010">{{cite book |last=Pigliucci |first=Massimo |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aC8Baky2qTcC&pg=101 |title=Nonsense on Stilts: How to Tell Science from Bunk |date=May 15, 2010 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-66787-4 |page=101}}</ref> On his blog [[Pharyngula (blog)|"Pharyngula"]], developmental biologist [[PZ Myers]] reviewed ''Lifecode'' and concluded that it was "a description of the development and evolution of balloon animals".<ref>{{Citation |last=Myers |first=PZ |title=Lifecode: From egg to embryo by self-organization |date=July 17, 2007 |work=Pharyngula |type=blog |url=http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2007/07/lifecode_from_egg_to_embryo_by.php |access-date=October 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070906043449/http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2007/07/lifecode_from_egg_to_embryo_by.php |archive-date=September 6, 2007 |url-status=dead |publisher=ScienceBlogs |author-link=PZ Myers}}</ref> In 2007, Pivar attempted to sue ''Seed Media'', whose [[ScienceBlogs]] hosted "Pharyngula", for describing him as "classic crackpot",<ref>{{Citation |last=Myers |first=PZ |title=Lifecode |date=July 12, 2007 |work=Pharyngula |type=blog |url=http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2007/07/lifecode.php |access-date=October 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070907142321/http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2007/07/lifecode.php |archive-date=September 7, 2007 |url-status=dead |publisher=ScienceBlogs |author-link=PZ Myers}}</ref> but the case was withdrawn after ten days.<ref>
{{cite book |last1=Delta |first1=George B. |title=Law of the Internet, Volume 1, 2009 supplement |last2=Matsuura |first2=Jeffrey H. |publisher=Aspen Publishers |year=2009 |pages=11–12}}</ref><ref>
{{Citation |last=Keim |first=Brandon |title=Pseudoscience not Selling? Just Sue a Science Blogger for Libel |date=August 20, 2007 |work=Wired Science |url=https://www.wired.com/2007/08/pseudoscience-n/ |access-date=October 5, 2011 |publisher=Condé Nast Digital}}</ref> 

On July 5, 2016 a scientific paper titled ''The Origin of the Vertebrate Body Plan in the Geometric Patterns in the Embryonic Blastula'' was published in the peer-reviewed journal ''Progress in Biophysics and Molecular Biology'' identifying Stuart Pivar as the principal investigator.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Edelman |first1=David B. |last2=McMenamin |first2=Mark |last3=Sheesley |first3=Peter |last4=Pivar |first4=Stuart |date=July 5, 2016 |title=Origin of the vertebrate body plan via mechanically biased conservation of regular geometrical patterns in the structure of the blastula |journal=Progress in Biophysics and Molecular Biology |volume=121 |issue=3 |pages=212–244 |doi=10.1016/j.pbiomolbio.2016.06.007 |pmid=27392530 |doi-access=free}}
</ref>

== Personal life ==
At [[The Factory]] in the early 1970s, Pivar met [[Andy Warhol]] who became one of his closest longtime friends.<ref name=":1" /> With Warhol he would go on regular shopping trips to buy "masterpieces", which could be objects bought anywhere, from a high-end auction house to a fleamarket.<ref>{{Cite journal
 |last=Alexander |first=Paul
 |date=27 January 1992
 |title=What happened to Andy's Treasures?
 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=gOMCAAAAMBAJ&q=Stuart+Pivar&pg=PA26 |journal=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]
 |page=28
}}</ref> After the artist's death in 1987, Pivar recalled that "Andy Warhol loved to buy art. We used to go shopping together for it for a few hours practically every day in the past couple of years."<ref>Russell W. Belk, ''Collecting in a consumer society'', Psychology Press, 1995, p.72</ref>

Pivar was also a well-known friend of the late financier [[Jeffrey Epstein]]. Pivar said the friendship ended after [[Maria Farmer]], the first person to report Epstein's crimes to law enforcement, informed him personally of the abuse. Farmer made her formal allegations in 1996 and also spoke to Pivar about the abuse at that time. She had graduated from the New York Academy of Art the previous year.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |title= Here Are the 3 Most Disturbing Takeaways From Mother Jones's Interview With Jeffrey Epstein's Art Advisor and Former 'Best Pal' |first= Ben |last= Davis |date= August 26, 2019 |work= [[Artnet|artnet news]] |url= https://news.artnet.com/art-world/stuart-pivar-jeffrey-epstein-art-advisor-1635133 |access-date= 2019-11-10}}</ref> Nonetheless, in 2003 Pivar wrote a note for [[Jeffrey Epstein's birthday book]], containing a limerick with the lines "Jeffrey at half century, with credentials plenipotentiary, though up to no good whenever he could, has avoided the penitentiary."<ref name="y635">{{cite web | last=Cascone"] | first=["Sarah | title=Epstein Birthday Book Exposes Art World Elites' Crude Tributes | website=Artnet News | date=2025-09-11 | url=https://news.artnet.com/art-world/epstein-birthday-book-letters-2686524 }}</ref><ref name="s990">{{cite web | last=Klee | first=Miles | title=We Read the Extremely Creepy Epstein Birthday Book So You Don't Have To | website=Rolling Stone | date=2025-09-10 | url=https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-features/jeffrey-epstein-birthday-book-letters-1235424033/ }}</ref> Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell were board members of Seed Media Group when Pivar sued it in 2007.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nally |first=Leland |title=Jeffrey Epstein, My Very, Very Sick Pal |date=August 23, 2019 |work=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]] |url=https://www.motherjones.com/crime-justice/2019/08/jeffrey-epstein-my-very-very-sick-pal/ |access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref>

=== Art collection ===
Pivar is a life long art collector.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theartnewspaper.com/news/collector-says-he-was-duped-into-selling-brancusi-sculpture|title=Collector says he was duped into selling Brancusi sculpture|last=Kenney|first=Nancy|date=July 19, 2019|website=www.theartnewspaper.com|access-date=2020-02-13}}</ref> He was a collector of 19th-century [[academic art]] at a time when it was unfashionable.<ref>''Art & antiques'', Volume 22, 1999, p.99</ref> A scholar of the work of the sculptor [[Antoine-Louis Barye]], he wrote "The Barye Bronzes: A Catalogue Raisonne" in 1974, a collation of critical commentary on all the sculptor's known works.<ref>
{{cite book
 |last1=Day |first1=H.T.
 |last2=Sturges |first2=H.

 |title=Joslyn Art Museum, paintings & sculpture from the European & American collections

}}</ref><ref>

 |title=19th century European paintings, drawings and sculpture
 |publisher=[[Sotheby's]]
 |page=265
}}</ref>
